description: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered invisible radiation capable of passing through matter. In a few months, medicine saw a revolution.

hero.hook: A hand, bones, a photo. Medicine will never again be blind.

blocks.text: **November 8, 1895**, in Würzburg (Germany), the physicist **Wilhelm Röntgen** notices a screen that shines... even though it is not affected by visible light. Something invisible crosses the room.
He calls this the **X** rays, the “X” meaning “unknown.” Within a few weeks, he photographed the bones of his wife's hand. Radiology was born.

Röntgen works with a tube where electrons hit a target. He covered the tube with black cardboard. However, a fluorescent screen glows from a distance. He understands that invisible radiation comes out of the tube.

blocks.caption: The famous image: the hand bones and the wedding ring.

blocks.text: Röntgen never filed a patent on X-rays. He wanted all science to be able to use them freely.

blocks.caption: Very quickly, doctors and armies used X-rays.

blocks.text: Before, to “see” a fracture or a bullet, you often had to open it. With X-rays, we obtain an image of the interior without cutting. Hospitals and armies are adopting the technique at breakneck speed.
At first, we ignore the risks. Operators take x-rays for hours. Burns, then cancers appear. It will take time to understand that X-rays are powerful… and dangerous.
Today, we protect patients and caregivers: limited doses, lead aprons, strict controls.
X-rays paved the way for all modern imaging: scanners, industrial controls, and even the study of the structure of crystals (later useful for DNA).
In **1895**, Röntgen discovered X-rays, an invisible radiation that passes through matter. Medicine is gaining a new perspective... on condition that the risks are controlled.
